title: Project's pathways towards impact
content:
# B.2.1 Project's pathways towards impact

The project's central result is a reusable observation chain, not a single assessment. It carries measurement from molecules to satellites along one agricultural pressure gradient. The chain, its protocols and its models are released under open terms, so others run them after the project ends. The topic BIODIV-01 asks for this framework as a Research and Innovation Action. The destination Biodiversity and ecosystem services sets the longer-term impacts it must serve. Each result below maps to a topic outcome first, then to a destination impact.

## (a) Unique contribution to the topic outcomes

The topic sets three expected outcomes, and the project answers each with a specific result rather than with research in general.

- First outcome, fit-for-purpose assessment and trend prediction. The project delivers European-scale habitat and ecosystem classification and trend predictions that carry the uncertainty the case benchmarks measured (D6.2, D6.3). A prediction without that uncertainty is not fit for a protection or restoration decision.
- Second outcome, capacity through integration across sensors and platforms. The project specifies one multisensory integration architecture (D2.2) and joins the molecular layer to the in-situ and satellite record through a published metadata standard. A genomic observation and a satellite observation of the same place become queryable together (D5.3).
- Third outcome, in-situ data usable for training and validation. The project reworks a multi-season field archive into a documented training and validation resource with a declared split protocol (D6.1). Site, season and treatment travel together into one fold, so a reused model cannot learn the site and pass as though it learned the biology.

One design choice drives the contribution across all three outcomes: a single pressure gradient. The gradient runs from farmland, through the freshwater ecotones that receive its runoff, to the coastal waters downstream. The three demonstration cases therefore share one pressure and one measurement protocol. A harmonisation decision taken for farmland is tested twice more, in realms that did not design it (D4.4). A single-realm study cannot run that test. This is evidence of integration rather than an assertion of it.

## (a) Contribution to the longer-term destination impacts

The destination sets six expected impacts in the longer term, and the project maps a pathway to all six.

- Knowledge of biodiversity status, trends and drivers improves, because one measurement culture now spans three realms and extends to European coverage (OC3, OC6).
- Methods and tools become available and used. The joint protocols, the crosswalk package, the provenance-tracked pipeline and the classification models are released under FAIR terms to the European Open Science Cloud and the common data spaces (D3.1 to D3.4, D6.2).
- The biodiversity crisis is better understood, because the land-to-coast pressure pathway becomes observable, with the molecular layer joined to it (WP5).
- Reporting authorities and stakeholders receive evidence in the form their obligations take, because a reporting-needs assessment runs before the outputs are designed (D7.1).
- Farmers and land managers receive biodiversity indicators inside the farm-management tools they already use, through an existing multi-country user network (D7.2, D7.3).
- Progress on international commitments becomes countable, because every habitat label carries a crosswalk to the European classification and a global ecosystem typology, and occurrence records reach the global data facilities the topic names (D3.2, D3.4).

The project delivers availability. It measures reuse rather than promising it, so a group outside the consortium can apply the released methods without asking the consortium for anything.

One clause of the fourth destination impact is only partly addressed. The project improves the evidence a biodiversity valuation rests on. It runs no valuation and claims none, because no partner carries environmental economics.

## Target groups that benefit

The pathway reaches distinct groups, each through a specific output.

- Ecosystem-assessment research groups and biodiversity machine-learning researchers reuse the labelled training resource and the reproducible benchmarks (D6.1, D6.2).
- Biodiversity data-infrastructure operators and the standards bodies that maintain the European habitat classification and the global ecosystem typology receive the harmonisation decisions, each with its disposition recorded (D3.4).
- Competent authorities carry reporting obligations under the Habitats Directive, the Birds Directive, the Marine Strategy Framework Directive and the EU Nature Restoration Regulation. They receive outputs shaped to those obligations (D7.1, D7.2).
- Farmers, land and sea managers, and the agricultural holdings in the user network receive indicators they can act on, and are asked whether they can (D7.3).
- The international biodiversity assessment community receives occurrence records and crosswalked labels countable in a global assessment (D3.4).
- Policymakers and the interested public receive plain-language evidence on the biodiversity crisis, distinct from the reporting outputs above.

## Quantified estimates

The project fixes twelve impact indicators. Each measures something the project delivers and controls, and each names one deliverable.

| Indicator | Deliverable |
|---|---|
| Prioritised biodiversity knowledge gaps, each paired with its named data need | D2.1 |
| Observation datasets delivered under one protocol, one per ecosystem realm | D4.1 |
| Harmonisation decisions tested in a realm that did not design them, and the share that survived | D4.4 |
| Classification benchmark scores per case under the declared split, with uncertainty | D6.2 |
| European-scale maps and trend predictions published with stated uncertainty | D6.3 |
| Training and validation sets published with a reproducible benchmark | D6.1 |
| Datasets and services registered in the open science cloud and the common data spaces | D3.4 |
| Share of habitat labels resolving to both the European classification and the global typology | D3.2 |
| Harmonisation decisions submitted to the standards bodies, with disposition recorded | D3.4 |
| Reporting obligations for which an output is accepted without rework | D7.1 |
| Holdings evaluating the indicators, and the share reporting they could act on them | D7.3 |
| Molecular records joinable to an in-situ and a satellite record of the same place | D5.3 |

No target numbers are fixed yet. A target is a consortium commitment, and partner participation is not yet confirmed. The consortium sets the numbers at grant preparation, so each indicator reads as a measured quantity rather than a guess.

## (b) Requirements and barriers beyond the project's scope and duration

Several conditions sit outside the project's scope and its 48-month duration. Each can change over time, so the project treats each as a measurement, not a promise.

- Other R&I and standards adoption. The framework's long-term reach depends on standards bodies adopting the harmonisation decisions, and the project cannot adopt them on their behalf. It submits each decision with its disposition recorded (D3.4) and holds a standing cooperation interface to the named in-situ data frameworks and to the FuturEO programme (WP1). An unresolvable habitat label is reported to those bodies, not forced into a mapping.
- Evolving typologies and metadata standards. The European classification and the global typology change over time. The crosswalk package (D3.2) is versioned and republished, so a label stays resolvable after a classification is revised.
- Regulatory environment. The value of reporting-shaped outputs depends on the reporting obligations staying as the directives and the Nature Restoration Regulation define them, and those obligations may change. The reporting-needs assessment (D7.1) runs first and is repeatable, so outputs track the obligation rather than a fixed template.
- Targeted markets and user behaviour. An indicator changes no farming decision unless a practitioner acts on it. The usability evaluation asks whether a holding could act, and reports a negative result rather than hiding it (D7.3). The route to practitioners runs through one partner's user network, and if that network is unavailable the project states the loss rather than absorbing it.
- Data availability beyond the consortium. Environmental DNA reference libraries may be incomplete for the taxa the cases need. The project builds reference sequences for the gap taxa and reports the share of reads left unassigned (WP5). Required satellite bands or revisit frequencies may be unavailable from the European programmes, whose use is an eligibility condition for this topic. The project records every additional source and the reason the European data did not cover the need.

Critical risks inherent to project management, including consortium confirmation and the budget route, are addressed in the Implementation section, not here.
